title: Quantities and safe measurement

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain quantities and safe measurement
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Voltage is energy per charge; current is charge flow per second. Resistance relates voltage to current for an ohmic component. A voltmeter measures a difference between two nodes. An ammeter interrupts the branch so current passes through it.
worked: For 12 V across 15 kΩ, I = 12/15000 = 0.0008 A = 0.8 mA = 800 µA. The prefix changes the number, never the physical quantity.
procedure: Power OFF before moving any leads or changing the circuit. Choose a DC voltage range above the source; wire the voltmeter in parallel and the ammeter in series. Predict current, then compare the signed reading with the prediction. Power OFF again before rewiring.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is placing an ammeter directly across a voltage source a fault?
checkpoint.answer: It creates a low-resistance path rather than measuring the intended branch.

title: Resistor colour codes and tolerance

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain resistor colour codes and tolerance
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Four-band resistors use two digits, a multiplier and tolerance; five-band resistors use three digits, a multiplier and tolerance. Tolerance describes a permitted interval, which includes the nominal value.
formulas: Rnom = digits × 10^multiplier; Rmin = Rnom(1-t); Rmax = Rnom(1+t)
worked: Red-black-black-red-brown gives 200 × 100 = 20000 Ω ±1%. Its permitted interval is 19800 to 20200 Ω. Gold means ±5%; red means ±2%.
procedure: Read the bands in order. Turn sources off and isolate the resistor before measuring resistance. Compare the measurement with both tolerance limits.

checkpoint.prompt: Can a nominal 470 Ω, ±5% resistor measure exactly 470 Ω?
checkpoint.answer: Yes. The full interval 446.5 to 493.5 Ω includes nominal.

title: Potentiometers and breadboard nodes

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain potentiometers and breadboard nodes
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: A potentiometer has two end terminals and a wiper. At a fractional wiper position x, the ideal segment resistances sum to the end-to-end resistance. Breadboard connectivity must come from actual row and rail wiring; apparent proximity is insufficient.
formulas: RAW = x RAB; RWB = (1-x) RAB; RAW + RWB = RAB
worked: For RAB = 10 kΩ and x = 0.3, RAW = 3 kΩ and RWB = 7 kΩ. With 10 V across the ends and no wiper load, VWB = 7 V under this explicit x convention.
procedure: Identify end terminals with power off. Sweep the wiper and measure each segment. Use actual breadboard node mapping to check continuity; do not assume rails cross a physical split.

checkpoint.prompt: What happens to end-to-end resistance as an ideal unloaded wiper moves?
checkpoint.answer: It remains constant; only the two segment resistances change.

title: Series DC circuits

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain series dc circuits
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Series components form one path and carry the same current. Voltage drops add algebraically around the loop. Choose polarities before calculating so Kirchhoff’s voltage law has a consistent sign convention.
formulas: Req = ΣR; I = Vs/Req; Vk = I Rk; Vs - ΣVk = 0
worked: With 12 V, 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series, Req = 3 kΩ and I = 4 mA. The drops are 4 V and 8 V; 12-4-8 = 0 V.
procedure: Construct the specified single path. Measure source current in series and each voltage across its resistor. Complete a VIR table and check the KVL residual.

checkpoint.prompt: Does the current get used up after the first resistor?
checkpoint.answer: No. A steady series branch carries the same current throughout.

title: Parallel DC circuits

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain parallel dc circuits
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Parallel branches share both end nodes and therefore share voltage. Conductances add. Total current is the signed sum of branch currents, not an average. Adding a positive-resistance branch reduces equivalent resistance.
worked: At 10 V across 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ and 5 kΩ, currents are 10, 5 and 2 mA. Itotal = 17 mA and Req = 588.235 Ω. Product-over-sum is only a two-resistor shortcut.
procedure: Build common source and return nodes. Measure each branch with a series ammeter and verify common voltage with a parallel voltmeter. Complete the KCL table.

checkpoint.prompt: Can product of all resistances divided by their sum solve three parallel resistors?
checkpoint.answer: No. Use the reciprocal sum, which also has the correct dimensions.

title: Mixed series and parallel networks

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain mixed series and parallel networks
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Reduce only subnetworks whose endpoints really match. Find the source current through a series section, then recover the parallel voltage and branch currents. A meter’s position changes the measured quantity.
formulas: Rp = 1/Σ(1/Rbranch); Req = Rs+Rp; Vp = Vs Rp/Req; Ik = Vp/Rk
worked: A 1 kΩ series resistor feeding 2 kΩ || 2 kΩ has Req = 2 kΩ. At 12 V, Itotal = 6 mA, Vparallel = 6 V and each branch carries 3 mA.
procedure: Draw the actual nodes before wiring. Measure before and after the split and across the shared branch nodes. Complete the VIR table and identify an intentionally open branch.

checkpoint.prompt: Where does the source ammeter go to measure total current?
checkpoint.answer: Before the branch split, in the common series path.

title: Power and efficiency

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain power and efficiency
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer. A resistor dissipates positive power when current enters its positive-voltage terminal. Rated power is a model limit; also respect configured voltage limits and derating. Efficiency compares useful output with total input.
formulas: P = VI = I²R = V²/R; energy = P t; η = Pout/Pin
worked: At 12 V across 1 kΩ, I = 12 mA and P = 0.144 W. A 0.125 W part is overloaded under this model. If useful output is 0.12 W from 0.15 W input, efficiency = 80%.
procedure: Measure voltage and current before computing power. Compare each component with its configured rating. Sweep the supply only within equipment limits and record protection events.

checkpoint.prompt: May individual-source powers be added in superposition?
checkpoint.answer: No. Superpose signed voltages or currents first; power is nonlinear.

title: Node voltages and multiple sources

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain node voltages and multiple sources
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: Ground is the chosen voltage reference. Vab = Va - Vb can be negative. Source polarities matter. Only combine ideal voltage sources in series or ideal current sources in parallel when the actual topology permits it.
formulas: Vab = Va - Vb; Σloop V = 0; series equivalent Vs = signed ΣVs
worked: If Va = 3 V and Vb = 8 V relative to the same reference, Vab = -5 V. Two opposed series sources 12 V and 5 V drive 7 V across a 1 kΩ load, giving 7 mA.
procedure: Mark one common reference and every source polarity. Build the assigned supported series-source network and measure signed node differences. Never parallel conflicting ideal voltage sources.

checkpoint.prompt: Does a negative voltage prove the meter is broken?
checkpoint.answer: No. It indicates the measured polarity is opposite to the chosen reference direction.

title: Superposition

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain superposition
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: A linear network response is the signed sum of its independent-source contributions. Deactivate an ideal independent voltage source with a short and a current source with an open; preserve internal impedances. Do not deactivate dependent sources.
worked: Two 10 V sources each feeding one 1 kΩ resistor into a 1 kΩ load give Vload = 6.6667 V. Each source acting alone contributes 3.3333 V. Compute load power from the combined voltage.
procedure: Build the original multi-source network. Record the full response, then safely replace each inactive ideal voltage source with its stated zero-voltage model. Restore all sources and compare signed contributions.

checkpoint.prompt: Should powers from the individual-source runs be summed?
checkpoint.answer: No. Sum voltage/current contributions, then calculate the final power.

title: Thévenin equivalents

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain thévenin equivalents
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: A linear two-terminal network can be represented by open-circuit voltage Vth and series resistance Rth. Specify the load port first. Remove the load to find Vth; use deactivated independent sources and a test source to determine Rth.
worked: A 12 V source with 1 kΩ series and 2 kΩ shunt has Vth = 8 V and Rth = 666.667 Ω. With RL = 1 kΩ, Iload = 4.8 mA and Vload = 4.8 V.
procedure: Disconnect the load at the named port. Measure open-circuit voltage, then power off and use the specified resistance method. Build the equivalent circuit and compare both under the same load.

checkpoint.prompt: May Rth be found by shorting an energized physical supply?
checkpoint.answer: No. Deactivate sources through the supported safe procedure before resistance measurement.

title: Maximum power transfer

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain maximum power transfer
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: For a linear DC Thévenin source with positive finite resistance, load power peaks at RL = Rth. Maximum load power does not mean maximum efficiency; equal source and load resistance dissipate equal powers. Enforce actual component limits.
formulas: PL = Vth² RL/(Rth+RL)²; RL,opt = Rth; Pmax = Vth²/(4Rth)
worked: For Vth = 14 V and Rth = 4 kΩ, Pmax = 196/16000 = 0.01225 W = 12.25 mW at RL = 4 kΩ. This is an original explicit-port example, not an adoption of unseen source topology.
procedure: Sweep load resistance below, at and above Rth. Record voltage, current and power in a table. Plot power against load resistance and locate the peak.

checkpoint.prompt: Is load power largest at a short circuit?
checkpoint.answer: No. A zero-ohm load has zero voltage and zero ideal load power.

title: Source conversion and cumulative DC analysis

source.basis: Supplied complete text audit and documented concept ranges; original authored example
source.visual_gate: Unseen source-specific diagrams and breadboards excluded

objectives: Explain source conversion and cumulative dc analysis
Predict signed quantities in base SI units
Construct, measure and reconcile the assigned supported network
explanation: A voltage source in series with resistance is port-equivalent to a current source in parallel with that same resistance. Preserve polarity and current direction. Equivalence holds at the external terminals; internal branch quantities need not match.
formulas: In = Vth/Rth; Vth = In Rth; Rn = Rth
worked: A 10 V source with 2 kΩ series resistance becomes a 5 mA source injecting into the positive port with 2 kΩ in parallel. A 2 kΩ load receives 5 V and 2.5 mA in either model.
procedure: Construct the voltage-source network and its Norton equivalent with the installed adjustable current-source modules. For solver current a→b connect the physical minus terminal to node a and plus terminal to b. Record voltage and current at suitable loads, check that each source remains in CC within its stated compliance, and compare port behavior. Use the host-captured actual electrical state; never substitute calculation results for meter observations.

checkpoint.prompt: Does selecting current limit on any CV/CC supply create an ideal independent current source?
checkpoint.answer: No. Compliance and operating region constrain real source behavior; use the correct supported model.
